prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of a family owned business called GCP, which produces golf clubs in the United States. They used to produce clubs that were easy to use, so most of their customers are beginner players. They recently received a patent for a new club that would enhance the performance of amateurs and professionals alike. Product innovation is paramount in this industry and they want help capitalizing on this development with a strong product launch.
prompt.question: Help the CEO of GCP plan a strong product launch for their new patented golf club. You will work through several phases: analyzing the market, deciding whether to build a new plant or expand the current one, identifying other decision factors, identifying key implementation risks, and pricing an insurance policy against construction delays.

clarifying_info.q: What production methods does GCP currently use?
clarifying_info.a: GCP currently uses liquid production only. Some competitors use solid production.

clarifying_info.q: What is the estimated demand for the new club?
clarifying_info.a: Demand is estimated at 60,000 sets over the next few years.

clarifying_info.q: Are the two plant options mutually exclusive?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — either build a new additional plant or expand the current plant.

exhibits.title: Golf Club Sets Sold by Year and Production Type
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of golf club sets sold from 2007 to 2011 (2007–2008 historical, 2009–2011 estimated), broken down by category: Solid (for professionals), Other Liquid (for amateurs), and Top 10 Liquid producers.

data.note: Top 10 Liquid commands a dominant share across all years; total market more than doubles from 2007 to 2009.

framework: Phase 1 — Market analysis: assess market size, growth rate, and competitive dynamics (liquid vs. solid, top vs. other producers)
Phase 2 — Capacity decision: compare total machine costs for a new plant vs. expanding the current plant to meet 60,000-set demand
Phase 3 — Qualitative factors: management/admin, product quality, distribution, event risk, future capacity, implementation timing, impact on existing lines
Phase 4 — Implementation risks: timing of launch and construction cost overruns
Phase 5 — Insurance pricing: calculate expected loss and gross-up for insurer margin

questions.prompt: Phase 1 Q1: What do you observe about this market from the exhibit?
questions.guidance: The market has been growing rapidly — more than 100% in roughly two years (2007 to 2009). This makes it an attractive market to enter with a new product. Both liquid and solid segments are expanding.

questions.prompt: Phase 1 Q2: Does being one of the top liquid producers matter? Why?
questions.guidance: Yes. The Top 10 Liquid producers command a disproportionately large share of the market. Possible reasons: (a) economies of scale in production, distribution, and advertising; (b) greater capacity to invest in product innovation — which is stated to be paramount in this industry.

questions.prompt: Phase 2: Should GCP build a new additional plant or expand its current plant to meet estimated demand of 60,000 sets?
questions.guidance: Compare machine costs for each option that exactly or minimally exceeds 60,000 sets. The one-time investment of $2M is identical for both options and can be ignored in the comparison. Find the cheapest combination of machines that meets demand.

math.setup:
Demand = 60,000 sets. One-time investment of $2M is the same in both cases — ignore it.

NEW PLANT options (max 3 lines; Machine I = 2,000 sets/month = 24,000/yr at $12.5M; Machine II = 1,250 sets/month = 15,000/yr at $8M):
- Option A: 2× Type I + 1× Type II → production = 2×24,000 + 15,000 = 63,000 sets; cost = 2×$12.5M + $8M = $33M
- Option B: 3× Type I → production = 72,000 sets; cost = 3×$12.5M = $37.5M (over-budget)
- Option C: 1× Type I + 2× Type II → production = 24,000 + 30,000 = 54,000 sets — insufficient
Optimal new plant: 2× Type I + 1× Type II = $33M, 63,000 sets.

EXPAND CURRENT PLANT (Machine I = 1,250 sets/month = 15,000/yr at $8M; Machine II = 7,500 sets/year at $5.5M; note 1,250/month = 15,000/year so Type I >> Type II efficiency):
- 4× Type I → production = 4×15,000 = 60,000 sets; cost = 4×$8M = $32M
- Alternative with Type II machines would require 8× at $5.5M = $44M — much worse
Optimal expansion: 4× Type I = $32M, exactly 60,000 sets.
steps: New plant optimal: 2× Machine I + 1× Machine II → 63,000 sets @ $33M
Expand plant optimal: 4× Machine I → 60,000 sets @ $32M
Difference: $33M vs $32M — roughly the same (~$1M difference)
One-time $2M investment is identical and cancels out
Conclusion: costs are essentially equal; decision requires qualitative factors
math.answer: New plant costs ~$33M; expansion costs ~$32M. Costs are roughly equivalent, so the decision cannot be made on cost alone.

questions.prompt: Phase 3: Given roughly equal costs, what other factors should inform the build-new vs. expand decision?
questions.guidance: Brainstorm pros and cons across multiple dimensions. Strong answers cover: Management/Admin (one plant = lower labor and G&A costs), Product quality (easier to maintain standards at one location), Distribution (two plants may lower distribution costs if geographically advantageous), Event/operational risk (two plants diversify risk and may lower insurance costs), Future capacity (new plant provides ~3,000 extra sets/year headroom), Implementation timing (new plant may take longer), Impact on current lines (expansion may disrupt existing production).

questions.prompt: Phase 4: The CEO decides to expand. Assuming market estimates are 100% correct, what are the two main issues keeping the CEO up at night regarding the expansion project?
questions.guidance: Timing: product innovation is paramount and the market is expanding rapidly, so launching on time is critical — any construction delay directly threatens market share. Construction costs: the CEO needs assurance that expansion costs won't escalate beyond the budget after commitment. Both relate to project execution risk (schedule and cost overruns).

questions.prompt: Phase 4 follow-up: How could the CEO protect himself against those risks?
questions.guidance: The CEO could purchase an insurance policy to hedge against cost overruns and/or delay-related revenue losses.

questions.prompt: Phase 5: GCP has contracts to sell 60,000 sets at $500 each. If GCP cannot produce more than 90% of 60,000 sets in the next eight months, it loses 10% of contracts — this happens with probability 20%. If it produces 90% or more, it loses nothing. The insurer operates with a 10% margin. What is the insurance price?
questions.guidance: Calculate from the insurer's perspective: expected loss = probability of bad outcome × loss amount, then gross up for margin. The key insight is that the 10% margin means expected loss = 90% of premium.

math.setup:
Loss scenario (prob 20%): GCP loses 10% of contracts.
Loss amount = 10% × 60,000 sets × $500/set
No-loss scenario (prob 80%): loss = $0
Insurer margin = 10%, so expected loss = 90% of premium.
steps: Expected loss represents 90% of premium (insurer keeps 10% margin)

brainstorming.prompt: Given that calculated costs for building a new plant vs. expanding are roughly the same, what other issues would you want to analyze? What are the pros and cons of each option?

categories.name: Management and Administration
ideas: Single plant reduces labor costs and G&A overhead
Two plants require duplicate management structures

categories.name: Product Quality
ideas: Easier to enforce quality standards with one plant
Two plants risk inconsistency across production runs

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Two geographically dispersed plants may reduce shipping costs to different regions
Single plant may create logistics bottleneck for nationwide distribution

categories.name: Event Risk
ideas: Two plants diversify against fire, natural disaster, or equipment failure
Insurance premiums may be lower with two locations due to risk diversification

categories.name: Future Capacity
ideas: New plant provides ~3,000 extra sets per year of headroom above the 60,000 target
Expansion exactly meets demand — any upside would require further investment

categories.name: Implementation
ideas: Construction timeline — new plant may take longer to build and commission
Expansion may disrupt current production lines during construction

categories.name: Strategic Flexibility
ideas: Second plant could serve a different geography or customer segment
Selling or leasing surplus capacity at a second plant if demand falls short

recommendation: GCP should proceed with expanding the current plant at a cost of ~$32M (4× Machine I lines), which exactly meets the 60,000-set demand forecast and is marginally cheaper than a new plant
If future demand signals strengthen, GCP can revisit a second plant; the current expansion preserves capital while meeting near-term needs
risks: Construction cost overruns could erode the slim cost advantage of expansion
Timing delays during expansion could cause GCP to miss the product launch window in a fast-growing market
Market demand could exceed 60,000 sets, leaving no capacity buffer with the expansion option
next_steps: Purchase an insurance policy (estimated ~$667K premium) to hedge against production shortfall due to construction delays
Establish fixed-price construction contracts to cap expansion cost risk
Develop a phased launch timeline that accounts for construction lead time and production ramp-up
